**MainCity Bakery (MB) **

MB is a small bakery that produces bread. Yasin started the bakery 6 months ago with help from the government. Yasin needed a business plan to support his application for government help. An extract from the business plan Yasin produced is shown in Appendix 1. The market research was carried out by Yasin. He asked a small sample of family and friends to fill in a questionnaire. Yasin’s business plan also contained forecast data. 

MB’s bread is freshly-made every day in the bakery, which is located at the back of MB’s small shop. The bread is then sold the same day. Yasin has 2 employees to help him produce the bread and 1 employee to serve customers in the shop. All employees work 5 days a week and are paid the legal minimum wage. Yasin uses a democratic leadership style. 

Yasin needs to keep costs low to be competitive. He uses packaging that cannot be recycled. Yasin also buys the cheapest ingredients, most of which are imported. He is planning to use lean production in the bakery but he has to decide which method to use. 

MB’s main competitors advertise that they only use ingredients from local suppliers. Yasin is thinking of changing the suppliers he uses for ingredients and packaging. He wants MB to have a good ethical image which he could use in advertising. 

Yasin plans to start making cakes. He is considering two options as outlined in Appendix 2. MB’s fixed costs will increase as there will be additional expenses whichever option he chooses.

{align=center} **Appendix 1 **

{align=center} **Extract from Yasin’s business plan for MB**

| Section | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Market research | Questionnaire results are as follows: - Bread is eaten by all age groups
- Of the sample asked:
- 85% want products made using ingredients from local suppliers
- 70% want to purchase cakes as well as bread from a bakery |
| Resources | - \$10 000 to buy bakery equipment
- Rent for the bakery and shop each month
- \$3000 for start-up supplies and ingredients |

{align=center} **Appendix 2 **

{align=center} **Forecast data for MB’s cake options**

|   | **Option 1 ****Small cupcakes** | **Option 2 ****Large birthday cakes** |
| --- | :---: | :---: |
| Monthly sales of cakes | 4000 | 100 |
| Variable cost per cake | \$0.50 | \$10 |
| Additional fixed cost per month | \$3000 | \$3000 |
| Price per cake | \$2 per cupcake | \$60 per birthday cake |
| Gross profit margin | 75% | 83.33% |
| Sales growth | Low | High |

{align=center} **Appendix 3 **

{align=center} **Packaging supplier advertisement**

{align=center} We only supply packaging made from sustainable sources. 

{align=center} This will keep your products fresh and protect the environment. 

{align=center} We can deliver your packaging when you need it

Explain **one** benefit and **one** limitation to Yasin of using a break-even chart.

Refer to the following [insert](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/jun-2022-paper-2-case-study---new.pdf) when answering the question.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that it shows the MB's break-even output **[K]**. This means Yasin will know how much bread he needs to sell each month to cover all his costs. For example, if the chart shows he needs to sell 1000 loaves **[Ap]** to break even, Yasin can plan how much equipment and ingredients he needs **[An] **to make sure MB produces at least this amount. This will help him avoid making a loss **[An]**

However, a break-even chart assumes all the bread produced will be sold **[K]**. MB may not sell all its bread in a day, and some may go to waste. The costs of producing unsold bread **[Ap] **are not taken into account on the chart. If the chart is inaccurate, at a specific output shown, MB might actually be making a loss instead of breaking even or making a profit, despite what the chart suggests **[An]. **This may affect the business's ability to survive **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Write two full paragraphs, one for each reason/point
> - In each paragraph:
> 
>   - State one valid point relevant to the question → 1 K mark
>   - Apply it clearly to the case study → 1 Ap mark
>   - Explain how it works using a cause–effect chain → up to 2 An marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Relevant benefits might include:
> 
>   - Shows break-even output – so Yasin knows how much bread he needs to sell to break even – this will allow him to plan the bakery and equipment required – to ensure at least the minimum quantity of bread is produced and sold
>   - Shows the margin of safety – this is the amount of bread Yasin predicts will be sold above the break-even output – it provides a target for sales  of bread – so that MB makes a profit
>   - Helps in decision making – so that Yasin knows the minimum target amount of bread to produce – he can see if he needs to increase the price to break-even more quickly – or if lower ingredient costs is  required by MB to make a profit
>   - Shows the area of profit or loss – and therefore what the output needs to be to cover all costs – if the market research shown in the business plan does not indicate that sufficient sales will be made to make a profit – then Yasin may need to think again about his plans for the bakery.
> - Relevant limitations might include:
> 
>   - A break-even chart assumes all the output will be sold/provides an estimate of sales – but MB may not sell all the bread in the day – some may be wasted and the costs of producing these will not be taken into account – so at a specific output the business may not make a profit but may make a loss
>   - The break-even chart is drawn on the assumption of straight lines – but when the output is higher Yasin may be able to bulk buy ingredients – this may mean he can receive discounts so the variable cost per unit may not be constant
>   - Fixed costs/variable costs may change – if the scale of production changes as the bakery expands – the rent or depreciation of equipment will change/ingredient costs may change
>   - Need a separate break-even chart for each product/need a new chart if prices are changed – relevant if going to make cakes
> - Application could include:
> 
>   - Bread; bakery; cakes; data presented in Appendix 2; fixed costs will change if either of the options in Appendix 2 go ahead

FO has been a private limited company for 20 years. It is owned and run by the Chan family and is located in country Z. In country Z the secondary sector has become relatively more important as the country has developed. FO is a manufacturer of wooden furniture that is suitable for outdoor use. Its products include tables, chairs and other outdoor furniture.

Customers order online from the FO website. The furniture is then delivered to customers in country Z using FO’s own delivery vehicles. However, FO is considering changing to selling its furniture through either wholesalers or large retailers in country Z.

The Chan family have the business objective of contributing to sustainable development. FO only uses sustainably sourced wood when making furniture. This is from local forests in country Z and the wood is more expensive than imported alternatives.

For many years FO shareholders have reinvested profits to provide the finance for growth. FO recently took over 2 other furniture businesses in country Z and plans further takeovers. The Chan family plan to continue to control and manage FO after this expansion. The leadership style of these two companies is very different to that of FO and their factories are located several miles away from FO in different regions of country Z.

FO need to manage all its resources effectively. It tries to use the same components such as nails, brackets and paint for all its furniture designs. It is important to not run out of raw materials and so orders to suppliers must be carefully planned to avoid late deliveries. FO want to keep wastage of materials to a minimum. FO also need to consider how many employees are required to complete each order.

Appendix 1 - FO website advertisement

![A wooden garden arbor seat with a pitched roof, lattice sides, and a bench underneath. The structure is made of light-colored wood and designed for outdoor use.](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/51323_0450-june-2021-insert-paper-2-cie-igcse-business.png)

{align=center} **Appendix 3**

{align=center} **Newspaper article from the Daily News April 2021**

{align=center} **Sustainable production needed to save the planet**

A report from the International Committee for the Planet states that manufacturers must find more sustainable ways to produce their products as global warming is becoming more of an issue

The report suggests three main ways manufacturers can change:

- Only use raw materials from sources that replace what they have used. This is estimated to raise variable costs by 20%
- Only use packaging that can be recycled. Costs are estimated to increase but the selling price may not rise by more than 10%
- Only use electric vehicles to deliver products. The cost of buying electric vehicles is more than petrol or diesel vehicles. Using electric vehicles could enable variable costs to be reduced by 5%.

Calculate the margin of safety per month for tables.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/0450-june-2021-insert-paper-2-cie-igcse-business---new.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solution_md:
**20 units** **[2]**

**Calculation steps**

State the formula to calculate the margin of safety

$\mathrm{Margin} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{safety}=\mathrm{Actual} \mathrm{sales}--\mathrm{Break}-\mathrm{even} \mathrm{level} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{sales}$    **[1]**

Subtract the break-even level of sales from the actual sales

$\mathrm{Margin} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{safety}=100\mathrm{units}--80\mathrm{units}\,\,=20\mathrm{units}$    **[1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The margin of safety is always expressed in units, or tables in this example

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (Margin of safety = Actual sales – break-even level of sales)
> - Forecast sales per month 100 – 80 (1) = 20 (1)

{align=center} **Everyone Theatre (ET)**

Zane and Zaara are both actors. They plan to start up a theatre in a low-income area of Main City. Zane and Zaara believe that helping the community is as important as being successful entrepreneurs.

The theatre will be a private sector business and Zane and Zaara have to decide whether to start up as an unincorporated business (partnership) or as a limited company. Zane is planning to prepare a cash-flow forecast for the first year. Zaara knows they will need to set business objectives for the theatre and also decide on a leadership style to use when managing employees. ET will have 24 part-time employees as shown in the organisational chart in Appendix 1.

Zane and Zaara plan to put on performances in the evenings for local people and tourists. There will be 100 seats in the theatre but not all the seats will be sold if the price is too high. The Marketing Manager, Zaara, will need to decide which performances to put on, what price to charge and which refreshments to sell. Zaara will also need to decide between the two possible options for the first performance when the theatre opens. Information on the two options is shown in Appendix 2.

In the daytime the theatre building will be used by Daycare, a local social enterprise. Daycare takes care of young children up to the age of 5 so that low-income family members can go out to work. It also provides education for the children which helps their development and progress before they start school. Some of Daycare’s objectives are different to those of ET.

{align=center} **Appendix 1 **

{align=center} **Proposed organisational chart for the theatre**

![Organizational chart with a Marketing Manager overseeing Backstage (6), Actors (10), and Promotion (2), and a Finance and Administration Manager overseeing Cleaners (3) and Ticket Office (3).](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/47830_jun-2023-paper-2-case-study-v2---new.png)

Note: The numbers in brackets are the number of part-time employees who work in each department.

{align=center} **Appendix 2**

{align=center} **Forecast data for the two possible options for ET’s first performance at the theatre**

| **For each performance** | **Option 1** | **Option 2** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Number of actors/employees | 7 | 24 |
| Average wage cost per actor/employee | \$30 | \$10 |
| All other costs including scenery, costumes and promotion | \$1000 | \$2000 |
| Forecast revenue assuming all 100 seats are sold | \$1000 | \$2500 |

{align=center} **Appendix 3 **

{align=center} **Email from Zane to Zaara**

**To: Zaara **

**From: Zane **

**Date: 1 April 2023**

We want to support the local community and we need to make decisions about the following. 

Should we: 

- Pay fair wages even though they may be higher than those paid by competing theatres?
- Only buy costumes produced in the local community?
- Purchase all refreshments from suppliers that do not pollute the environment?

Using Appendix 2 and other information, consider the two options for the first performance at the theatre. Which is the best option for Zaara to choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/jun-2023-paper-2-case-study-v2---new.pdf)when answering the question.
parts.solution_md:
Looking at the financial aspects, Option 2 is more profitable

Option 1: Revenue: \$1000 Costs: (7 × \$30) + \$1000 = \$1210 Profit: \$1000 - \$1210 = -\$210 (loss) **[Ap]**

Option 2: Revenue: \$2500 Costs: (24 × \$10) + \$2000 = \$2240 Profit: \$2500 - \$2240 = \$260 **[Ap]**

Option 2 makes a profit of \$260 per performance, while Option 1 results in a loss of \$210. Therefore, choosing option 2 would align with ET's objective of being a successful business **[Ap]**, capable of providing rewards for its entrepreneur owners, Zane and Zaara, who took a risk in establishing the theatre business **[An]**

Moreover, Option 2 employs more actors (24 compared to 7 in Option 1) **[Ap]**. This supports ET's goal of helping the community **[Ap]** by providing more job opportunities. This could enhance ET's reputation and encourage customers to buy tickets for performances, in the knowledge that they are supporting a good cause [An]

However, Option 2 has a higher ticket price (\$25 compared to \$10 in Option 1) **[Ap]**. This might be a concern as ET is located in a low-income area, meaning few locals would be in a position to visit the theatre regularly, limiting revenue **[An]**. The higher revenue allows, though, for better wages (\$10 per actor) **[Ap]** and more spending on costumes and scenery (\$2000) **[Ap]**, which could result in a higher-quality performance **[An]**

Option 2 is the best choice for ET's first performance, as it balances profitability with community support **[E]**, aligning with ET's objectives of being successful entrepreneurs and helping the community** [Ap].** Option 1 results in a financial loss of \$210 per performance, provides fewer job opportunities with only 7 actors **[Ap]**, and doesn't match ET's planned organisational structure. Option 1's lower ticket price **[Ap]** seems more suitable for a low-income area, but it's not financially viable **[E]**. Option 2, despite its higher ticket price, offers a better balance of profitability and community benefit, making it the most appropriate choice for ET's first performance **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Option 1 – simple, low-cost production**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Fewer actors needed → total variable costs fall → cheaper performances
>     - Scenery and costume cost \$1000 less → total cost per show \$1210 → frees budget for other needs
>     - Ticket price \$10 per seat → likely to sell all 100 seats → makes estimated revenue more reliable
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Average wage per actor is \$20 higher → raises labour cost per show
>     - Loss of \$210 each performance → unsustainable without changes
>     - Revenue \$1000 per show → lowest income of the two options
> - **Option 2 – larger, higher-quality production**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Wage cost per actor only \$10 → labour expense is lowest
>     - Profit \$260 per show → best return among both options
>     - Revenue \$2500 per performance → \$1500 more than Option 1
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Needs 17 more actors → total wage costs are highest
>     - Total cost per show \$2240 → big upfront expense
>     - Ticket price \$25 → risk of unsold seats if demand is weaker than expected
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - Option 1 minimises costs and uses a low ticket price → helps fill seats but runs at a loss per performance
>   - Option 2 delivers higher revenue and a positive profit per show → risks fewer sales at a higher ticket price and heavier production costs
